new_entities.name: Paternal zinc repletion
new_entities.description: Zinc supplementation or restoration of zinc adequacy in men before conception.

new_entities.name: Sperm motility
new_entities.description: The ability of sperm to move effectively, including total or progressive motility.

edges.effect_quant: The most current network meta-analysis found zinc among the better-ranked options for total motility in 2,045 men with idiopathic OAT, but direct trial data are inconsistent. One older smoker-infertility study reported improved sperm quality after zinc therapy in 125 men, whereas a placebo-controlled OAT trial in 83 men found no meaningful motility benefit after accounting for placebo effects.
edges.population: subfertile men or men with impaired semen parameters receiving zinc supplementation before attempted conception
edges.mechanism: Zinc is involved in antioxidant defenses, chromatin stabilization, and sperm-membrane function, so repletion is biologically plausible when baseline status is low or exposure burdens are high. The inconsistent trial results suggest that benefit probably depends on deficiency, co-exposures, or whether zinc is used alone or inside a broader antioxidant regimen.
edges.summary: The safest interpretation is that zinc repletion may help sperm motility in some men, but the evidence is not consistent enough to treat it as a dependable stand-alone fix. This is best framed as a context-dependent, low-to-moderate-certainty male-fertility intervention.
edges.caveats: Many studies combine zinc with other antioxidants or include special populations such as smokers or severe OAT cases. Baseline zinc status is often poorly characterized, which makes it hard to distinguish true repletion from empiric supplement stacking.

evidence.notes: Effect of antioxidants on semen parameters in men with oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia: a network meta-analysis.
The micronutrient supplements, zinc sulphate and folic acid, did not ameliorate sperm functional parameters in oligoasthenoteratozoospermic men.

evidence.citation: Omu AE et al 1999 Arch Androl
evidence.notes: Chronic cadmium toxicity to sperm of heavy cigarette smokers: immunomodulation by zinc.
